“I learned from a peddler who, while traveling through your part of the country this winter, had a tooth pulled, that Bovary was still working hard. That does not surprise me, and he showed me his tooth; we had coffee together. I asked him whether he had seen you; he told me no, but that he had seen two animals in the stable, from which I conclude that business is going well. So much the better, my dear children, and may the good Lord send you every happiness imaginable.

“It grieves me not yet to know my beloved little granddaughter Berthe Bovary. For her I have planted, in the garden beneath your room, an oat-plum tree, and I do not want anyone to touch it, except to make preserves for her later, which I shall keep in the cupboard for her when she comes.

“Farewell, my dear children. I embrace you, my daughter; you too, my son-in-law, and the little one, on both cheeks.

“I remain, with many compliments,

“Your loving father,

“THEODORE ROUAULT.”

For several minutes she remained holding the thick paper between her fingers. The spelling mistakes intertwined with one another, and Emma followed the gentle thought that chattered throughout it like a hen half hidden in a thorn hedge. The writing had been dried with ashes from the hearth, for a little gray dust slipped from the letter onto her dress, and she almost thought she could see her father bending toward the hearth to pick up the tongs. How long it had been since she had sat beside him, on the stool in the chimney corner, when she would burn the end of a stick in the great flame of the crackling sea rushes!...

She remembered summer evenings filled with sunlight. The foals neighed when anyone passed and galloped, galloped... Beneath her window there was a beehive, and sometimes the bees, wheeling in the light, struck against the panes like rebounding golden balls. What happiness there had been then! What freedom! What hope! What an abundance of illusions! None remained now! She had spent them on all the adventures of her soul, throughout every successive condition, in virginity, in marriage, and in love—thus continually losing them along the course of her life, like a traveler who leaves something of his wealth at every inn along the road.

But what, then, was making her so unhappy? Where was the extraordinary catastrophe that had turned her life upside down? And she raised her head, looking around her as though to seek the cause of what was making her suffer.

An April sunbeam shimmered on the china on the shelf; the fire was burning; beneath her slippers she felt the softness of the carpet; the daylight was white, the air mild, and she heard her child bursting into laughter.

Indeed, the little girl was then rolling on the lawn amid the grass that was being made into hay. She lay flat on her stomach atop a haycock. Her nurse held her by the skirt. Lestiboudois was raking nearby, and each time he approached, she leaned forward, beating the air with both arms.

“Bring her to me!” said her mother, rushing to kiss her. “How I love you, my poor child! How I love you!”

Then, noticing that the tips of her ears were a little dirty, she quickly rang for hot water, cleaned her, changed her linen, stockings, and shoes, asked a thousand questions about her health, as though she had returned from a journey, and at last, kissing her again and weeping a little, placed her back in the servant’s hands; the woman remained quite dumbfounded by this excess of tenderness.

That evening, Rodolphe found her more serious than usual.

“It will pass,” he judged. “It is a whim.”

And he then failed to keep three appointments in a row. When he returned, she showed herself cold and almost disdainful.

“Ah! You are wasting your time, my pretty one...”

And he appeared not to notice her melancholy sighs or the handkerchief she took out.

It was then that Emma repented!

She even asked herself why she hated Charles so, and whether it would not have been better if she could have loved him. But he offered little purchase for such revivals of feeling, so that she remained greatly perplexed in her faint impulse toward sacrifice, when the apothecary came at just the right moment to provide her with an opportunity.




XI


He had recently read a eulogy of a new method for curing clubfeet; and since he was a partisan of progress, he conceived the patriotic idea that Yonville, in order to keep abreast, ought to have strephopodic operations.

“For,” he said to Emma, “what does one risk? Consider”—and he enumerated the advantages of the attempt on his fingers—“almost certain success, relief and improvement in the patient’s appearance, fame quickly acquired by the operator. Why, for example, should your husband not wish to rid that poor Hippolyte, from the Lion d’Or, of his affliction? Bear in mind that he would not fail to tell every traveler of his cure, and then”—Homais lowered his voice and looked around him—“who could prevent me from sending the newspaper a short notice about it? Ah, good Lord! An article circulates... people talk about it... it ends by snowballing! And who knows? Who knows?”

Indeed, Bovary might succeed; nothing assured Emma that he was not skillful, and what satisfaction it would be for her to have urged him into an undertaking by which his reputation and fortune would be increased? She asked only to lean on something more solid than love.

Charles, pressed by the apothecary and by her, allowed himself to be persuaded. He sent to Rouen for Doctor Duval’s volume, and every evening, with his head in his hands, he immersed himself in the book.

While he studied equinus, varus, and valgus—that is, strephocatopodia, strephendopodia, and strephexopodia (or, more plainly speaking, the different deviations of the foot, whether downward, inward, or outward)—together with strephyopodia and strephanopodia (in other words, twisting beneath and bending upward), Monsieur Homais, with all manner of arguments, exhorted the inn servant to undergo the operation.

“You will perhaps feel scarcely more than a slight pain; it is a mere prick, like a little bloodletting, less than the excision of certain corns.”
